abstract: This paper traces how the term 'woke,' originating in the Black community as 'stay woke' for anti-racism consciousness, was politicized into a 'culture war' epithet across Twitter and YouTube between 2012 and 2022. Drawing on identity politics and polarization theory, the authors use computational user- and content-level analyses to show how partisan opinion leaders and their followers hijacked social justice discourse both separately (via distinct platform affordances) and synergistically (via cross-platform coordination). Findings reveal that culture war framing came to dominate 'woke' discourse across every user group, with conservatives especially engaged in coordinated cross-platform amplification of right-wing content.
key_claims: Social justice discourse originating in marginalized communities (e.g., 'stay woke') can be hijacked and politicized by partisan opinion leaders over time, becoming culture war fodder.
Politicization plays out both differently across platforms (via distinct affordances and user bases) and synergistically (via cross-platform coordination).
The term 'woke' shifted markedly away from its consciousness-raising origins toward culture war and political framing across all user groups, including liberals and Black opinion leaders.
Conservatives exhibit a coordinated, asymmetric cross-platform information ecosystem, with YouTube serving a content 'supply' role and Twitter a 'demand' role for right-wing content.
The Black community's declining use of 'stay woke' suggests the term became so politicized that its originators grew reluctant to use it.
methods: Collected data from Twitter (Twitter API v2) and YouTube (tuber R package) using 'woke'-related search terms from January 2012 to December 2022; final datasets of 18,378,315 tweets from 5,974,144 users and 35,445 videos from 17,398 channels.
Segmented data into three periods: T1 (2012–2015, pre-2016 election), T2 (2016–May 2020, pre-George Floyd BLM), T3 (May 2020–2022).

User-level analysis: applied Vintage Sparse Principal (VSP) component analysis to partition the Twitter retweeting network into 74 clusters, then manually coded opinion-leader clusters; identified top 222 YouTube channels accounting for 90% of views via long-tail distribution and manually coded them.

Content-level analysis: used BERTopic modeling (with LDA as validation) on video titles (n=35,445) and a 10% sample of unique tweets (n=604,968) to identify topic categories, then predicted topics across all unique tweets.

URL extraction: extracted and unshortened embedded URLs in tweets (N=1,777,556) and YouTube video descriptions (N=88,591), grouping them into Twitter, YouTube, and Other domains to trace cross-platform link-sharing.
Statistical tests: two-tailed Z-tests comparing proportions across platforms and Chi-square tests with standardized residuals to examine topic distribution shifts by user group over time.
findings: H1 rejected: political opinion leaders were more prevalent on YouTube (conservative news/commentary drew 65.41% of views) than Twitter overall; however, liberals were significantly more prevalent on Twitter while conservatives dominated YouTube.
H2 supported: politicized topics (Culture Wars + Politics) made up 67.72% of tweets but only 23.46% of YouTube videos, where lifestyle/entertainment dominated (56.99%).
Across all Twitter user groups and phases, discourse shifted toward Culture Wars and away from Stay Woke; Black opinion leaders' engagement in culture wars reached 69.22% by T3.
On YouTube, Culture Wars grew across nearly all channel categories, and Politics rose especially among conservative channels (0% at T1 to 16.95% at T3).

Cross-platform: YouTube links appeared in 7.06% of Twitter links, while Twitter links appeared in 9.88% of YouTube links; conservatives on Twitter shared YouTube content more than liberals, often to redefine or ridicule 'woke.'

Facebook was the second-largest URL domain on both platforms; right-wing outlets (Fox News, Breitbart, NYPost, Daily Mail) appeared in Twitter's top 'Other' domains but not YouTube's, indicating coordinated right-wing promotion.
contributions: Demonstrates the longitudinal politicization of a social justice term (from #StayWoke to anti-woke culture wars) using large-scale computational analysis over a decade.
Advances cross-platform / comparative social media studies by showing both the distinct and combined roles of Twitter and YouTube in politicizing social identity.
Documents an asymmetric right-wing cross-platform information ecosystem where YouTube supplies content and Twitter amplifies it.
Empirically supports theories of identity-politics-driven polarization and the co-optation of marginalized communities' discourse by partisan actors.
framing: The paper situates itself at the intersection of identity politics, political polarization ('culture wars'), and comparative/cross-platform social media studies, drawing on scholarship about affective polarization, opinion leadership, platform affordances, and the co-optation of social justice discourse (e.g., Mason, Cammaerts, Zavattaro & Bearfield). It positions social media as a battleground where marginalized-community framings are hijacked by partisan actors, extending single-platform politicization research to a multi-platform, longitudinal perspective.
